items.title: Rethinking trust AI visibility in public services.
items.abstract: This article argues that trust in AI-mediated public services depends not only on whether systems are accurate, fair, or efficient, but on how their presence is made visible to the people affected by them. Across welfare, healthcare, and border governance, artificial intelligence increasingly shapes decisions about access, movement, support, and rights. Yet these systems often operate within familiar institutional procedures, making their role difficult to see, interpret, or challenge. The article develops the idea of AI visibility to explain how different forms of disclosure shape public trust. It distinguishes between invisible AI, partially visible AI, and fully disclosed AI, showing how each can produce different responses: misplaced confidence, confusion, suspicion, or informed challenge. By shifting attention from technical performance alone to the public experience of decision-making, the article shows that trust is shaped by whether people can understand where authority lies and how decisions are made. Foregrounding visibility helps reframe debates on algorithmic governance, institutional legitimacy, and accountability. In an increasingly automated state, the question is not only whether AI systems can be trusted, but whether their role in public decisions can be meaningfully seen. Working paper (Version 1.0). This manuscript has not yet undergone peer review.

items.title: SAFE AND ETHICAL AI-BASED SELF-HEALING MENTORING FOR STUDENTS OF SMP NEGERI 30 MUARO JAMBI
items.abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) provides opportunities for students to use technology as a tool to support self-reflection and emotional management. However, its use in the context of mental health requires an understanding of safety, ethics, privacy, and technological limitations. This community service program aimed to provide assistance to students in utilizing AI as a self-healing support tool in a safe, ethical, and responsible manner. The program was conducted at SMP Negeri 30 Muaro Jambi and involved 30 students and a school guidance and counseling teacher as a partner. The program employed a Participatory Action Research (PAR) approach through four stages: preparation, core implementation, evaluation, and sustainability. The activities included orientation and initial assessment, emotion and stress recognition, overthinking management, self-healing techniques, AI-assisted self-reflection, and education on the ethics and safety of AI use. Participant responses were evaluated among 24 students using a 1–4 scale instrument covering material comprehension, usefulness, delivery, media, comfort, application of knowledge, and interest in future activities. The evaluation results showed an overall mean score of 3.43 out of 4.00, equivalent to 85.74%, which was categorized as very good. The highest score was found in participants' interest in attending similar activities in the future (90.91%), while all evaluation indicators remained in the very good category. The program indicates that practice-based assistance can help students understand AI as a support tool for self-reflection while strengthening their awareness of privacy, safety, ethics, and the limitations of AI in the context of mental health. Program sustainability is directed toward integrating the materials into school guidance and counseling services and continuing support through the school guidance and counseling teacher.

items.title: Secure Multi-Agent Collaboration Using Large Language Models
items.abstract: As Large Language Models have emerged and become increasingly significant, the way to develop smart multi-agent systems has been transformed, enabling them to communicate, collaborate and decision more efficiently. These systems rely on agents working independently which need to effectively and safely coordinate their actions, to maintain reliability in messy realworld environments. However, bringing LLMs into the mix introduces new risks like data leaks, trickery from bad actors, and trust issues. This paper breaks down a full plan for keeping multi-agent teamwork secure when using LLMs. We look at everything from how they are built and the rules they use to communicate to the safety tools used to stop attacks. We also talk about where this is being used now, the hurdles we still face, and where the tech is headed for building secure AI ecosystems

items.title: SHAPING SELF-REGULATED AND METACOGNITIVE LEARNING THROUGH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND LEARNING ANALYTICS
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics are increasingly embedded in educational systems, yet their implications for self-regulated learning (SRL) and metacognitive development remain only partially understood. This study conducts a systematic literature review of 34 empirical and review articles investigating AI-driven learning analytics in formal education settings, focusing on their impact on SRL, motivation, and academic performance. Following PRISMA-aligned procedures, the review identifies studies involving AI-based analytics tools, standardized SRL or metacognitive assessments, and empirical designs with pre–post or comparison data. The results indicate that AI-driven systems such as predictive models, adaptive platforms, chatbots, and generative AI can strengthen core SRL processes, increase motivation and engagement, and improve academic outcomes across diverse subjects and educational levels. However, the review also reveals persistent implementation challenges, including infrastructural limitations, teacher preparedness, privacy and ethical issues, and potential over-reliance on AI that may weaken independent strategic thinking. The article concludes that AI-driven learning analytics can meaningfully support SRL when embedded within coherent pedagogical frameworks and supported by institutional policies, and it outlines directions for future research on mechanisms, equity, and long-term effects.

items.title: Should AI Trust Its Gut? The Cost of Deliberative Moral Reasoning in Humans and AI
items.abstract: People prefer deliberation to intuition, when judging how others solve hard problems, and they extend this to artificial agents. Yet in the moral domain, the preference may reverse as intuitive moral responses appear to signal good character. One explanation is that fast, intuitive responses show real emotional engagement. Since machines are thought to lack emotion, it is unclear whether a preference for intuition in the moral domain extends to AI. Across three preregistered studies (N = 2,173), we find that it does, but that it appears to be driven by commitment to moral norms and precedents rather than emotion. In Study 1, participants preferred intuitive reasoning for moral decisions and systematic reasoning for non-moral decisions, for human and AI agents alike. Intuitive moral reasoning signalled better character but was not clearly expected to produce better outcomes. In Study 2, the character preference persisted when the AI was described as being incapable of emotion. In Study 3, we held the decision fixed and varied how firmly the agent held the relevant moral norm. An agent who would never reconsider applying a moral norm was rated above one who would reconsider given sufficiently high stakes; and both above one who weighed costs and benefits case by case. Commitment raised character ratings more than expected-outcome ratings. The character-based cost of moral deliberation appears to be a cost of treating a moral norm as negotiable, and we found strong evidence that people apply this inference to machines and people alike.

items.title: SMART E-LEARNING PLATFORM USING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
items.abstract: Online learning platforms provide access to educational content, but many systems deliver the same material to every learner andoffer limited support for identifying individual learning needs. This paper proposes a Smart E-Learning Platform using ArtificialIntelligence (AI) that aims to personalize learning through learner profiles, progress tracking, recommendation methods,automated practice feedback, and a dashboard for learners and instructors. The proposed workflow collects learning activity andassessment results, processes relevant learning indicators, and recommends suitable resources or practice activities. Possible AImethods include rule-based recommendation as a baseline, content-based filtering, and supervised models when sufficientlabelled data is available. The platform is designed as an academic prototype and should be evaluated using measurableindicators such as recommendation relevance, task completion, learner satisfaction, and usability. No implementation results orimprovement percentages are claimed in this proposal. Privacy, transparency, accessibility, and instructor oversight areimportant requirements. The system is intended to support teaching and learning, not to replace teachers or make high-stakesdecisions about students

items.title: Sociological_and_Psychological_Implications_of_AI_Infofagia
items.abstract: The advent and rapid spread of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Generative Artificial Intelligencesystems have marked an epistemological and structural discontinuity in the Information Society.While the early phases of the digital transition were characterized by processes of digitization, indexing,and heuristic data retrieval — where the machine acted primarily as an archivist or intermediary towardprimary content —, the current configuration of algorithmic architecture responds to a qualitativelydifferent dynamic. Artificial Intelligence does not merely organize human knowledge; to function,learn its semantic structures, and provide real-time synthesis, it requires the continuous, massive, andsystematic assimilation of informational material produced by humanity.To describe this phenomenon of insatiable and structural nourishment, we propose here the analyticalcategory of «infofagia» (derived from the Greek root phagêin, "to eat", combined with the informationalprefix). AI infofagia does not constitute a mere computational phase of the machine — the technicalphase of training on datasets —, but rather a total sociological and psychological fact. It identifies anextractive and metabolic process in which humanity's entire cultural, scientific, artistic, andconversational production is converted into raw matter, "ingested" by mathematical models, digested,and finally returned in the form of synthetic and normalized output.Adopting the paradigm of infofagia allows us to overcome both purely deterministic readings oftechnology and apologetic visions tied to the alleged democratization of knowledge. Through theanalysis of empirical data, international case studies, and clinical-social feedback, this essaydemonstrates how the informational appetite of large algorithmic models is not neutral, but directlyretroacts upon economic structures, cultural diversity, and the psyche of the final consumer.

items.title: Sovereign AI in the Developing Global South: Volume III – Conflicts, Insurgencies, and Algorithmic Warcraft vs. Statecraft
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is collapsing the historical separation between statecraft and warcraft. This third volume of the series on Sovereign AI in the developing Global South examines how algorithmic systems are restructuring state authority in domestic governance and armed conflict. It first analyses "algorithmic statecraft": biometric digital public infrastructure and the risk of function creep, with India's Aadhaar and Kenya's Huduma Namba as cases, and predictive policing as a form of actuarial justice that can codify structural discrimination. The article then turns to "algorithmic warcraft": AI decision support systems used for target generation in Gaza, automation bias and the "triage trap" that hollow out meaningful human control, and bias in military AI. It traces the democratisation of lethality through commercial and AI-enabled drones in Myanmar, Sudan, Libya and the Sahel, Bangladesh's border-security modernisation in response to regional spillover, and generative AI as an instrument of cognitive warfare. It closes with the fractured diplomacy of the Global South in the UN Group of Governmental Experts on lethal autonomous weapons systems, and argues that sovereign resilience requires contextualised AI frameworks under strict civilian oversight together with a coordinated push for binding international norms.

items.title: Specification without determinism: Evaluation suites as the primary product artifact in AI-native development
items.abstract: While the practice of managing products to be delivered by means of large language models is growing rapidly and spreading, increasingly a new practitioner discourse is spreading in the field of product management. The PRD (Product Requirements Document), that for decades has been the core specification artifact of the function, would be replaced by the evaluation suite: a set of test cases scored by the evaluation environment of the product under development, the suite encoding in executable form what acceptable system behavior looks like. This simple statement is now almost a mantra in the practice of managing products, and so far has not been subject of any in-depth conceptual investigation. In the requirements engineering community for machine-learning-enabled systems, the challenges of specifying such systems have been analyzed in great detail, but this does not yet translate into practical artifacts and practices of requirements engineering that would be used by practitioners in industry. This paper attempts to specify in detail what is actually being replaced by the evaluation suite, and what corresponding problems and challenges are not addressed by the new artifact. The study is of a theoretical nature and builds on two streams of literature: requirements engineering for machine-learning-enabled systems, and measurement validity in artificial intelligence evaluation. First, we clarify that the PRD serves three separate purposes: defining requirements, coordinating stakeholders, and facilitating deliberation about product intent. We then argue that only the first of these functions is actually transferred to the evaluation suite. Next, we introduce the concept of specification residue, i.e. the portion of what has been specified that cannot be encoded in an executable form and therefore ends up in the black box of individual judgment. We identify three types of such residue. Finally, we introduce a contingency framework that specifies under which conditions of outcome measurability and process-constraint density eval-primary specification is appropriate. Our results indicate that executable specification may shift but not reduce the need for human product judgment, and, most importantly, that it removes the key artifact through which such judgment was previously recorded and contested.

items.title: Students’ Engagement in Extensive Reading Activities in English at University of Mataram
items.abstract: This study investigated students’ engagement in Extensive Reading activities among English Education students at the University of Mataram. It aimed to describe students’ behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement and to identify the factors influencing their engagement. Although previous studies have reported the benefits of Extensive Reading for language proficiency and motivation, relatively little research has simultaneously examined the three engagement dimensions and their contextual influences in Indonesian EFL higher education. A qualitative descriptive design was employed with ten students completing a questionnaire and five students participating in semi-structured interviews. The closed-ended questionnaire functioned only as descriptive supporting data, while the semi-structured interviews provided the main qualitative explanations; therefore, the study was not designed as mixed methods and did not use inferential statistics. The questionnaire was used to identify general patterns through descriptive frequencies and percentages, while the interviews provided more detailed explanations of students’ reading experiences. The findings showed generally positive engagement. Behavioral engagement was reflected in relatively strong participation and effort, although reading consistency remained the main challenge. Emotional engagement was shown through interest, enjoyment, motivation, and positive attitudes toward English reading. Cognitive engagement appeared through reading strategies, comprehension monitoring, reflection, and connections between texts and prior knowledge. Five factors influenced engagement: reading materials and personal interest, language difficulty, time and academic responsibilities, motivation and academic requirements, and reading autonomy and lecturer support. Overall, students’ engagement in Extensive Reading was shaped by interacting personal, textual, and academic conditions.

items.title: Subjective, Behavioral, and Physiological Responses to Cognitive Workload in Individuals with Chronic Non-Specific Low Back Pain and Healthy Controls
items.abstract: Abstract Background Cognitive workload can influence performance and physiological responses during computer-based work, but these responses remain insufficiently understood in individuals with chronic non-specific low back pain (CNSLBP). This study investigated subjective, behavioral, electromyographic, and cardiac responses to increasing cognitive workload in individuals with CNSLBP and healthy controls during a dual-task computer-based paradigm. Methods Thirty participants, including 15 individuals with CNSLBP and 15 healthy controls, completed four experimental conditions combining two typing-speed levels and two cognitive workload levels. Subjective workload was assessed using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX). Behavioral performance and typing errors were recorded, while physiological responses were assessed using facial electromyography (EMG) and heart rate. Outcomes were analyzed using mixed repeated-measures analysis of variance to examine the effects of experimental condition, group, and their interaction. Results Increasing task demands significantly increased perceived workload (F = 34.63, p < 0.001) and reduced behavioral performance (F = 31.12, p < 0.001), whereas typing errors did not change significantly. No significant between-group differences were observed in perceived workload or behavioral performance. In contrast, participants with CNSLBP exhibited significantly greater RMS activity in the corrugator supercilii and frontalis muscles (both p < 0.001), and a significant condition × group interaction was observed for corrugator RMS (p = 0.018). Heart rate did not differ significantly across experimental conditions or between groups. Conclusions Individuals with CNSLBP maintained subjective workload ratings and behavioral performance comparable to healthy controls but exhibited greater facial muscle activation during task performance. These findings suggest that maintaining performance under cognitive demands may require greater physiological effort in individuals with CNSLBP. Multimodal assessment combining subjective, behavioral, and physiological measures may provide a more comprehensive understanding of cognitive workload responses in people with chronic low back pain.

items.title: Sustainability Aspects of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Education: A Law and Economics Analysis
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming human societies. In the many attempts to capture the novel trend of AI entering in all aspects of human life these days, hardly any research covers sustainability aspects of AI encroaching society. In the teaching of sustainability, AI appears as an way to improve carbon footprint as for energy savings opportunities – for instance by using online resources instead of physical books, reducing cognitive load of tedious tasks that had to be performed in educational settings previously, such as sifting through many books to find applicable cases in law school etc. At the same time, AI may create enormous environmental costs – e.g., through its electricity consumption use for big data storage and analytics – but also sustainability challenges – e.g., through eternally-living algorithms and technical devices. This chapter proposes weighing the costs and benefits of AI in sustainability education. In a Law & Economics analysis, the advantages and disadvantages of AI in sustainability education will be compared in order to present a framework to harvest the benefits but prepare for coping with the downsides of AI in sustainability education. Future student learning experience enhancement and educational changes due to AI in the future will be prospectively anticipated in the discussion. The future of education may positively develop in less cognitive load and diligent learning-by-heart but shift towards creative solution finding, navigating through a digital online jungle and development social network skills to find the right tools in a growing ocean of mushrooming AI advancements.

items.title: Sustainability of Learning at Work: A Typology of Learners in an ICT Organisation
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose This study examines how the sustainability of learning at work varies within the same organisational context. The objective is to enhance understanding of sustainable learning at work by identifying learner typologies that demonstrate the diverse manifestations of workplace learning sustainability. Design The study draws on semi-structured interviews (n = 27) conducted with employees and managers in a Finnish ICT organisation. The concept of workplace learning is approached from a sociocultural perspective, with sustainable learning understood as continuous competence development supported by adequate resources, social interaction and opportunities to anticipate future learning needs. The data were analysed using a two-stage process combining thematic analysis and typification. Findings The analysis identified three distinct learner types: enthusiastic learners, exhausted learners and uncertain learners. The learner types exhibited variation across three dimensions of sustainable learning: knowledge sharing and interaction, management support, and anticipation of learning needs. Enthusiastic learners experienced learning as meaningful and manageable, indicating that sustainable learning was largely achieved. Among exhausted learners, sustainability was challenged by excessive workload and learning demands. For uncertain learners, sustainability was challenged by insecurity, limited participation in knowledge-sharing practices and difficulties in directing their competence development. Originality/value The study contributes to the research on sustainable learning at work by demonstrating how the sustainability of workplace learning varies between individuals even within the same organisational context. The findings highlight the importance of learning support, the affordances present within the workplace, and the role of employee agency in the process of shaping sustainable learning within the professional environment.

items.title: Teachers' Occupational Well-Being and Students’ Academic Engagement in Cagayan De Oro City Division
items.abstract: Teachers’ occupational well-being is associated with their capacity to sustain effective teaching and support students’ academic engagement. This study aimed to determine teachers’ occupational well-being and students’ academic engagement in select districts of Cagayan de Oro City Division during the School Year 2026–2027. The study described the respondents’ profiles, assessed their occupational well-being and student engagement, examined the relationships between these variables, and tested the moderating effect of the respondents’ profiles. It used a quantitative descriptive-correlational design involving two hundred and twenty (220) Grade 7 public secondary school teachers selected through universal sampling. Data were collected using a modified questionnaire and analyzed using frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation, Pearson Correlation, and multiple regression. Findings showed that job satisfaction was stronger than work-life balance, while workload stress was more pronounced than burnout. Emotional engagement emerged as the strongest dimension of students’ academic engagement. Job satisfaction and work-life balance were significantly related to student engagement. Workload stress showed no significant relationship, while burnout had a weak link only to emotional engagement. Class size and teaching experience affected these relationships, but the subject taught did not. The study concludes that teachers’ occupational well-being and students’ academic engagement are interconnected, although their relationships vary across specific dimensions and profile characteristics. School administrators and teachers are encouraged to strengthen work-life balance, manage workload stress and burnout, promote cognitive engagement, and provide support responsive to class size and teaching experience.

items.title: TESSA: A Governance-Oriented Custom GPT for SME Guidance under the EU AI Act: Design, Implementation, and Evaluation
items.abstract: The increasing adoption of generative AI presents new opportunities while raising AI governance and regulatory challenges, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) navigating the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act). To support AI governance education, this study developed TESSA, a governance-oriented educational artifact within the OpenAI Custom GPT environment. Following a design science research approach, TESSA was evaluated against baseline ChatGPT using 100 benchmark scenarios through governance alignment assessment, human expert review, and consistency testing. Preliminary LLM-assisted assessment showed governance alignment rates of 90% for TESSA and 83% for baseline ChatGPT, while independent validation by an AI regulation law practitioner yielded 71% and 70%, respectively. Human expert review indicated that both systems provided generally strong governance guidance, while TESSA maintained high consistency across repeated executions. The findings suggest that governance-oriented grounding can support structured, practical, and stable AI-assisted compliance guidance for SMEs. The study contributes (i) a governance-oriented Custom GPT artifact for AI governance education, (ii) a human-validated regulatory update mechanism, and (iii) a multidimensional evaluation framework for governance-oriented AI artifact.

items.title: The CTF is dead, long live the CTF? Exploring perspectives on AI and the recognition of skill in capture-the-flag competitions
items.abstract: Capture-the-flag (CTF) competitions are used across the security community to recruit talent, build skills and sustain a competitive culture. As AI agents increasingly solve CTF challenges, three positions have emerged: that the format is obsolete, that it should become a benchmark for human-AI collaboration, and that headline claims overstate what the saturation of introductory benchmarks shows. This debate has been driven mainly by capability benchmarks, while the views of those who design, run and play CTFs remain largely unexamined. We report an exploratory qualitative study based on six interviews (seven participants) and eleven anonymous written responses from experienced CTF organisers and players. We interpret their accounts using Bourdieu's concepts of field and capital, and, for learning, the notion of threshold concepts. Participants did not offer a single verdict. Some were strongly critical of AI-assisted solving in competition; others wanted AI to be embraced and built into CTFs; still others took positions that depended on context. Strongly critical positions were voiced more often in anonymous written responses, a reminder that such positions are situated in the circumstances in which accounts are given. Participants involved in competition-focused CTFs described rankings that increasingly reflect access to AI models and money, and a loss of the satisfaction that made competing worthwhile. From an educational perspective, participants described students who solved challenges quickly but could not explain how they had done so. Participants disagreed about whether CTFs are preparation for real-world practice or a sport, and this seemed closely related to the stance they took. Many saw the enforcement of anti-AI measures as feasible only in on-site CTFs, and also largely dependent on trust. Several participants expressed doubt about CTF results still signalling individual skill levels to potential employers. We propose that this exploratory study into CTFs indicates a wider problem for the security workforce: when a measure of skill becomes cheap and easy to automate, a community must renegotiate what counts as legitimate performance. We also discuss implications for skills development, competition governance and hiring.

items.title: THE EFFECTIVENESS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN IMPROVING STUDENTS’ CRITICAL READING SKILLS AT EFL STUDENTS OF SULTAN AGENG TIRTAYASA UNIVERSITY
items.abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in improving students’ critical reading skills in higher education. As digital technologies increasingly shape learning environments, AI offers potential to enhance higher-order thinking. This research employed a quantitative approach using a quasi-experimental one-group pretest–posttest design. The participants were 30 sixth-semester students enrolled in the Qualitative Research on ELT course at Universitas Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa, selected through purposive sampling. The instrument was a standardized critical reading test measuring students’ ability to identify main ideas, analyze arguments, evaluate evidence, detect bias, and draw conclusions. It included multiple-choice and short-response items to assess analytical comprehension. The treatment integrated AI-based tools for text analysis, summarization, argument mapping, and reflective questioning. Students also compared their interpretations with AI-generated feedback to enhance metacognitive awareness. The intervention was conducted over four meetings under guided supervision. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and a paired-sample t-test. The findings revealed a statistically significant improvement in students’ posttest scores compared to pretest results at the 0.05 level. These results indicate that AI can effectively support critical reading development and foster deeper engagement with academic texts in EFL contexts.

items.title: The Effects Of Transformational Leadership And Intrinsic Rewards On Job Performance: The Mediating Role Of Affective Commitment In Government Commercial Institutions
items.abstract: This study examines the effects of transformational leadership and intrinsic rewards on job performance, with affective commitment serving as a mediating variable, in Government Commercial Institutions in Indonesia. Public sector organizations face increasing demands to improve performance while maintaining bureaucratic accountability and regulatory compliance. Understanding the mechanisms that influence performance in such institutional settings is therefore essential. A quantitative explanatory approach was employed using survey data collected from 311 civil servants. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS. The results show that transformational leadership and intrinsic rewards positively and significantly influence job performance. Both variables also have significant positive effects on affective commitment, which in turn enhances job performance. Furthermore, affective commitment partially mediates the relationships between transformational leadership, intrinsic rewards, and job performance. These findings highlight the importance of leadership practices and intrinsic motivational factors in strengthening employee commitment and improving performance in public sector institutions. The study provides empirical evidence from Government Commercial Institutions in Indonesia and offers practical implications for performance management in bureaucratic contexts.

items.title: The Influence of AI-Powered Translation and Paraphrasing Tools on Academic Writing English Department: A Mixed-Methods Study
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered technologies are increasingly being employed to help EFL students with academic writing. However, research into the combined use of DeepL and QuillBot during the writing process is sparse. This study looks on students' use and perceptions of DeepL and QuillBot in academic writing. Using a mixed-methods design, quantitative data were gathered from 49 English Education students through a 35-item five-point Likert-scale questionnaire and analysed using descriptive statistics, while qualitative data were obtained through semi-structured interviews with nine participants and analysed thematically. The data revealed that both instruments were generally viewed positively. DeepL was mostly utilized for translation and phrase improvement during planning and drafting, while QuillBot helped with paraphrasing and editing. Students did not rely solely on AI results; rather, they critically analyzed and corrected generated texts. The study finds that DeepL and QuillBot serve as supportive tools that improve academic writing while allowing students to retain control over content and meaning.

items.title: The interplay of mathematics anxiety, academic grit and learning engagement: A random-intercept cross-lagged panel analysis
items.abstract: Mathematics anxiety, academic grit, and learning engagement are central to children's mathematics learning, yet their longitudinal interplay remains insufficiently understood. This study examined dynamic associations among these constructs by following 3354 Chinese third- to fifth-grade students across three waves: December 2024, June 2025, and December 2025. To capture dimension-specific processes, six random-intercept cross-lagged panel models were estimated by crossing two dimensions of mathematics anxiety (learning and evaluation) with three dimensions of learning engagement (behavioral, cognitive, and emotional). Results indicated that within-person increases in mathematics learning and evaluation anxiety were prospectively associated with decreases in subsequent academic grit and learning engagement across dimensions. Within-person increases in behavioral, cognitive, and emotional engagement generally predicted lower subsequent mathematics anxiety and higher academic grit. Academic grit showed reciprocal associations with mathematics anxiety and indirectly linked mathematics anxiety to subsequent behavioral engagement; however, corresponding indirect effects involving cognitive and emotional engagement were less consistent. Educational relevance and implications statement This study followed Chinese upper elementary school children over one year to understand how mathematics anxiety, academic grit, and mathematics learning engagement develop together. The findings showed that when children experienced higher levels of mathematics anxiety, whether during learning or evaluation, they tended to show lower subsequent academic grit and lower behavioral, cognitive, and emotional engagement in mathematics. In turn, greater engagement was followed by greater academic grit and lower mathematics anxiety. Moreover, behavioral, cognitive and emotional learning engagement were indirectly associated with lower subsequent mathematics evaluation anxiety through academic grit. These findings suggest that, in mathematics education, encouraging children to “try harder” or exert greater behavioral effort in mathematics is valuable but may not be sufficient. Teachers should also carefully design instructional materials and learning activities that foster children's emotional and cognitive engagement in mathematics. Such efforts may support the development of academic grit and potentially contribute to reducing mathematics anxiety, particularly in evaluation situations.

items.title: The Paradox of Subjective Complexity: Why AI Automation Fails to Mitigate Adoption Barriers in the Circular Economy
items.abstract: Despite AI-driven algorithms simplifying C2C resale platforms, adoption rates among target users (predominantly mothers) for unused baby products remain low. This study decodes this resistance by integrating the Theory of Planned Behavior and Protection Motivation Theory within a two-stage mixed-methods design (qualitative interviews, N = 37; quantitative survey, N = 670) identifies three patterns refining technology adoption frameworks. First, we reveal a “paradox of subjective complexity”: platform operational self-efficacy remains the strongest predictor of adoption intention, overriding objective technological ease and demonstrating a persistent decoupling between automated simplicity and subjective capability beliefs. Second, perceived AI functionality efficacy serves as a cognitive precondition that significantly enhances users’ internalization of social proof. Third, spatial and economic threats were indirectly associated with adoption intention through perceived platform value, suggesting a pragmatic, threat-coping pathway to circular economy participation. These insights offer actionable blueprints for policymakers and platform designers: collaborative interfaces, explainable AI (XAI), and user competence scaffolding.

items.title: The psychological effect of gamification mechanism in XR immersive environment on user willingness to behave
items.abstract: With the rapid landing of XR technology in the fields of architecture, education, medical and other fields, how to effectively guide user behavior through interaction design and content mechanism has become the core topic of human-computer interaction research. This paper examines how gamification mechanisms in an XR immersive environment influence users' behavioral intentions. Drawing on self-determination theory as the overarching framework and incorporating spatial narrative structure and the Octalysis framework, it systematically examines the mediating roles of the three basic psychological needs—autonomy, competence, and relatedness—in the immersive experience. The study uses a combination of literature review and theoretical analysis, and constructs a theoretical model of "gamification elements → psychological needs to meet → willingness to act" through the depth analysis of typical XR cases such as medical training, building space guide, safety education and other types of XR cases. The study suggests that XR's distinctive sense of presence and interactivity may amplify the psychological effects of gamification drivers, such as a sense of mission and progression, while excessive competition and manipulative design may undermine intrinsic motivation.

items.title: The Relationship Between Generative AI Dependency and Critical Thinking Disposition Among University Students
items.abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly changed the way university students access information, understand academic materials, develop ideas, and complete assignments. Tools such as ChatGPT provide students with quick explanations, summaries, and feedback that can support their learning processes. However, the increasing accessibility of these tools also raises concerns about students' potential dependency on AI and its relationship with their willingness to think critically and independently. This study aims to examine the relationship between generative AI dependency and critical thinking disposition among undergraduate students from various academic disciplines. Generative AI dependency refers to the tendency to rely excessively on AI tools when completing academic tasks or performing cognitive activities. Meanwhile, critical thinking disposition refers to an individual's willingness to evaluate information, examine evidence, consider alternative perspectives, question assumptions, and reconsider conclusions based on relevant evidence. This research uses a quantitative approach with a correlational and cross-sectional design. Data will be collected through online self-report questionnaires distributed to active undergraduate students who have used generative AI for academic purposes. The study will measure generative AI dependency as the independent variable and critical thinking disposition as the dependent variable. The collected data will be analyzed using statistical software, such as JASP, with Pearson's or Spearman's correlation analysis selected according to the characteristics of the data. The findings are expected to contribute to the fields of cognitive psychology and educational psychology by providing additional empirical evidence regarding the relationship between generative AI dependency and critical thinking disposition. The results may also help students, lecturers, and educational institutions better understand the importance of using generative AI responsibly while maintaining independent reasoning, information evaluation, and active cognitive engagement. Since the study employs a correlational design, its findings will indicate statistical relationships rather than establish a causal relationship between the two variables.

items.title: The Sustainability of AI Literacy: The Environmental Cost of Embracing Generative AI in Higher Education
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping teaching and learning in Higher Education (HE). It is central to the future of work; proficiency in the use of AI is now identified as a core employability competency and an in-demand skill for employers. Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) face a growing imperative to equip students with relevant skills, advancing their AI literacy and digital career readiness. Generative AI (GAI) tools are increasingly used in the classroom, by both staff and students, presenting a range of new challenges and opportunities for the sector. However, the integration of GAI into teaching and learning brings with it environmental costs. This chapter explores the sustainability issues posed by using GAI in the classroom and considers the implications for HEIs. It will discuss the inherent tension between meeting student needs for AI literacy, whilst also ensuring an ethical and sustainable approach to the use of GAI in teaching and learning. This chapter will argue that educators must not only teach with GAI tools as they are now an inevitable part of the future of work, but also teach about them, including their sustainability risks. The chapter concludes with recommendations for HEIs for the integration of environmental sustainability into teaching and learning surrounding GAI.

items.title: The Symbiotic Equation: Artificial Intelligence as a Catalyst for Sustainability Education and Research
items.abstract: The intersection of Artificial Intelligence and Sustainability offers a revolution in the way we address environmental emergencies and teach our children and grandchildren to tackle them. This final chapter details with the key relationship between the disciplines and suggests that AI is used to analyse complex data and model ecological systems, which is essential to solve problems such as climate change and resource depletion. The discussion is organised into three main points. The first is a discussion about the growing significance of AI as a tool for decoding the complexity of “wicked” environmental problems. Second, it highlights the top trends in the future such as AI-driven predictive modeling for climate tipping points, lifecycle assessments for circular economies and the emerging role of generative AI to redefine sustainability pedagogy and communication. Third, it emphasises some of the pressing research needs, including reducing AI’s own environmental impact, combating algorithmic bias to enable equitable solutions and designing effective pedagogies to use. In times of mounting pressure to meet climate objectives, this interconnectedness will emerge as a hallmark, and become the backbone, of a human intelligence-as-machine relationship, facilitated through precision education and cultivation, to build an equitable and regenerative future.

items.title: Theoretical Foundations of Artificial Intelligence-enabled Project Management: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming project management (PM) practices, yet the theoretical foundations of AI-enabled project management remain fragmented and insufficiently synthesised. Without clearer theoretical grounding, research in this area risks remaining largely descriptive and application-oriented. This study aims to identify, map, and explain the theoretical perspectives used in research on AI-enabled project management. A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The search covered Web of Science and Scopus and identified 712 database records published between 2015 and 2025. After screening and full-text eligibility assessment, 10 theory-oriented studies were retained as the core dataset. The analysis shows that AI-enabled project management does not rely on a single dominant theory. Instead, the reviewed studies draw on several theoretical perspectives, including decision and behavioural theories, task–technology alignment, dynamic capabilities, stakeholder theory, complexity theory, information economics, and fuzzy set theory. Across the reviewed studies, AI is most often conceptualised as decision support or as an augmentation of managerial capabilities. The reviewed studies also differ in how AI is specified, ranging from relatively specific technologies and functions, such as generative AI, fuzzy AI models, predictive analytics, and AI-enabled monitoring, to broader conceptualisations such as AI assimilation and sociotechnical AI systems. The study contributes by showing how theoretical lenses, specific theories, AI roles, explanatory mechanisms, and levels of analysis can be linked into explanatory chains. These chains are then aggregated into recurring explanatory configurations and emerging theoretical streams. AI technology / function types are used as an additional coding dimension to interpret technology-specific implications for project management. Given the small final sample of theory-oriented studies, the identified streams should be interpreted as emerging patterns within this body of literature rather than as definitive or generalisable classifications of the entire AI-enabled project management field.

items.title: Time-of-Day Distribution and Human Factors in Recent General Aviation Accidents and Serious Incidents in Türkiye
items.abstract: Human factors are important contributors to general aviation (GA) accidents and serious incidents; however, the potential role of time of day, fatigue, and individual chronotype in GA occurrences remains insufficiently described. This study primarily aimed to provide a descriptive characterization of the temporal distribution and human-factor involvement of these occurrences rather than to test causal circadian mechanisms. This cross-sectional study analyzed GA accident and serious incident reports from Türkiye (2018–2025) publicly available on the Transportation Safety Investigation Center website, of which 33 met the inclusion criteria. Variables extracted from each report included operation type, flight phase, reported fatigue, medical contribution, operational human factors, and local occurrence time. Events were grouped into four predefined time-of-day blocks and their distribution was assessed using a chi-square goodness-of-fit test.Among the 33 included events, 11 were accidents and 22 serious incidents. Most occurred during training operations (25/33, 75.8%) and during the landing phase (19/33, 57.6%). A focused narrative review of the final reports showed that 32 of the 33 included events (97.0%) involved operational errors or violations attributable to personnel actions or decision-making. The distribution across the four time-of-day blocks was statistically non-uniform (χ²(3)=12.45, p=0.006), with the highest concentration between 10:00 and 13:59 (17/33, 51.5%). Fatigue was explicitly reported in only one event, and no medical cause was identified as a contributing factor.The observed late-morning concentration should be interpreted cautiously as exposure data were not available. Although this study does not establish a causal relationship between circadian timing, chronotype, and GA occurrences, chronotype-schedule mismatch may be considered a hypothesis for future research.

items.title: Toward Sustainable Higher Education: A Critical Review of the Emerging Issues Induced by Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The emerging issues brought to the limelight through the widespread application of AI in higher education, affecting sustainable teaching and learning in higher education, are examined in this chapter. A meticulous, systematic review of the literature from inside and outside Africa was conducted with important inferences drawn from reports, articles and dissertations published between 2020 and 2025. Searching, organising, storing, and reusing articles in databases like Google, Google Scholar, Web of Science, Science Direct, and the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) are all part of the systematic review process. Most importantly, this chapter presents a novel understanding of the products associated with the emerging issues of using AI in higher education. The findings revealed data privacy concerns, academic dishonesty, absence of AI solutions from the Global South, overreliance on technology, and lack of compliance with established policies and frameworks as emerging issues induced by AI use influencing sustainable higher education. The findings presented in this chapter underscored the importance of continuous counselling and awareness seminars and conferences with educators, students, and faculties on an institutional and faculty-wise basis as proactive measures to reduce the products of unethical use of AI in higher education. The authors posited and concluded by offering recommendations to manage the induced influence introduced by AI in higher education to achieve sustainable development goals prescribed by the United Nation’s Sustainable Development Goals.

items.title: Trustworthy Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Clinical Decision Support Systems: A Systematic Review of Methods, Validation, and Deployment Readiness
items.abstract: Registration status: This is a retrospective registration of a completed systematic review. The registration was created after completion of the literature search, study selection, data extraction, methodological-quality assessment, and evidence synthesis. It should therefore not be interpreted as a prospective preregistration. This systematic review evaluates trustworthy explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) for clinical decision support systems (CDSS), with particular emphasis on explainability methods, clinical validation, fairness, uncertainty, robustness, clinician involvement, governance, and real-world deployment readiness. The review methods, including the eligibility criteria, database search strategy, study-selection procedure, data-extraction domains, methodological-quality assessment, and synthesis approach, were defined a priori before the literature search and study-selection process. The review followed PRISMA 2020. Searches were conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, IEEE Xplore, and Embase for studies published from January 2018 through June 2026. The final searches were completed on 30 June 2026. Two reviewers independently performed study screening and data extraction, with disagreements resolved by consensus and, where necessary, consultation with a third reviewer. Methodological quality, risk of bias, and applicability were assessed using PROBAST+AI. Because of substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, the evidence was synthesized using a structured narrative approach and no quantitative meta-analysis was performed. No standalone formal review protocol was prospectively registered before commencement of the review. This OSF registration is being completed retrospectively to provide a transparent public record of the review methodology and to satisfy the registration requirements of the journal.

items.title: Utilizing Artificial Intelligence Tools to Support Pronunciation Practice Among Non-English Major EFL Students
items.abstract: Although AI-powered speech technologies have shown promise for L2 pronunciation learning, little is known about the efficacy of combining complementary AI-powered tools for out-of-class pronunciation practice among Vietnamese non-English majors, particularly in terms of aligning AI-based error detection and teacher assessment. This study investigates the integration of Speechify and Speechnotes to support pronunciation self-practice among 35 first-year non-English major EFL students at a public university in Vietnam. Data were gathered through a descriptive survey (N=35) and semi-structured interviews (n=10). Results showed that students responded positively to the simultaneous use of these two tools, with all interviewed participants expressing satisfaction and 85,7% valuing Speechnotes’ real-time visual feedback for error detection. Speechnotes’ error-detection capability also showed partial alignment with teacher judgments in identifying segmental errors, including omitted final sounds and vowel contrasts. Along with future advancements in AI tool features, this study offers valuable insights to improve the quality of pronunciation instruction for non-English major students, foster greater engagement and motivation in pronunciation practice, and ultimately support foreign language learning.

items.title: Value Orientation in Players: Development and Validation of a Tradeoff-Based Scale of In-Game Priorities
items.abstract: Players differ not only in what they enjoy but in what they prioritize when in-game goals conflict. Existing player-typology and motivation measures are additive and cannot capture which facet a player sacrifices under conflict. We develop and validate the Value Orientation (VO) scale, a tradeoff-based measure of in-game priorities across four dimensions: Efficiency, Exploration, Story, and Challenge. Each item embeds an explicit opportunity cost. Across three studies with Chinese players (total N = 813), exploratory factor analysis yielded a 16-item, four-factor scale, and confirmatory factor analysis in an independent sample replicated this structure (CFI = 0.99) and outperformed collapsed alternatives. The dimensions showed acceptable reliability, clear discriminant validity, theory-consistent convergent relations with needs and player-type measures, incremental validity beyond basic-needs satisfaction, prediction of choices on a differently worded situational task, full scalar invariance, and good retest stability. Known-groups evidence was largely supportive.

items.title: VERA: A Responsible AI Dashboard for Assessing LLM Deployments in Light of the EU AI Act
items.abstract: Institutions that deploy large language models in regulated settings often need technical evidence of responsible AI practices before approving a deployment. COMPL-AI provides a technical interpretation of the EU AI Act that organises this evidence under six principle groups and eighteen technical requirements, twelve of which current benchmarks can measure. The benchmark suites that produce this evidence are typically operated from a command line, while the staff who approve deployments are non-engineers. We present VERA, an open-source self-hosted dashboard deployed to facilitate responsible AI processes within a large European bank. A reviewer selects a model and runs public benchmarks against it. VERA scores the twelve requirements that current benchmarks can measure and instruments the energy consumed by each evaluation, adding run-level evidence for environmental impact. We run four served open-weight models through the requirement pipeline, and the dashboard displays a score for each measurable requirement. A within-subject study then compares how participants read these benchmark results: from the raw output files in one condition, and through the VERA dashboard in the other. The dashboard reduced the time needed to perform the responsible AI assessment, reducing the time required from 56 seconds using raw files to 30 seconds using our dashboard, on average. Our dashboard scored highly (4.36 out of 5) on usefulness in the survey conducted within the organization. The dashboard and the study material are released publicly to promote replicability and reproducibility in different organisational contexts.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Visual perception study of AR-HUD systems: The role of information shape and driver age
items.abstract: This study mapped drivers’ perceptual sensitivity to unfilled AR-HUD shapes (triangle, circle, and square) across an ultra-wide horizontal eccentricity span of 79.95° (−23.82° to 56.13°) and a vertical span of 23.08° (−11.21° to 11.87°). Twenty licensed drivers, stratified into younger and middle-aged groups, completed a detection-response task at 351 collectively sampled positions while driving in a controlled 70-km/h straight car-following scenario. Minimum perceptible size (MPS) data supported a statistically informed division of the tested FOV into 14 segments. Perceptual sensitivity was highest within 5° eccentricity and decreased markedly beyond 48.32°. Younger drivers generally had lower MPS, although several upper and peripheral cells showed non-significant attenuation or reversal of this age-group pattern. Shape advantages were segment- and age-group-specific: squares showed lower MPS in several intermediate and right-peripheral comparisons, whereas localized triangle advantages occurred near the center and in the far-right periphery. Composite driving performance and DALI workload did not differ significantly by age group or shape; the middle-aged group reported lower 3D-SART supply–demand scores, and Average Pupil Diameter (APD) varied among shape conditions. A depth-adjustable geometric formulation converted absolute MPS into relative visual-angle thresholds. The resulting 14-segment shape and size references provide condition-bounded guidance for AR-HUD design.

items.title: What the submission does not show: Complexifying cognitive offloading in students' mathematical work with LLMs
items.abstract: A common concern is that using large language models (LLMs) lets students offload mathematical work that tasks are designed to elicit. Yet such claims often rest on outcomes (e.g., submitted solutions), rather than on evidence of students' work with LLMs. We followed 23 first-year linear algebra students as they solved three differently designed homework tasks with LLMs. Drawing on self-regulated learning and choice-affluent environments, we interpreted each of 429 prompts as a trace of a regulatory event and compared 59 chatlogs with the problem solutions the students submitted. Prompts formed five structures, casting the LLM mainly as a solver, explainer, or validator. The mix of structures shifted across the tasks, and ten of the 15 students who completed all three tasks changed their dominant structure. Most final submissions stayed close to LLM output, including those that followed exchanges in which students had explained, conjectured, and checked their own ideas. We conclude that an LLM-aided submission is not a trustworthy marker of students' offloading of the mathematical work, and that offloading needs to be examined in each regulatory space and part by part rather than as a whole.

items.title: When college students perceive GAI feedback as credible: the role of perceived GAI feedback credibility in promoting deep learning through cognitive engagement
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has rapidly developed in higher education and has raised new questions from an educational psychology perspective. Why does GAI feedback promote meaningful learning for some college students but fail to produce similar learning benefits for others? To answer this question, this study develops a theoretical framework based on Information Processing Theory, Elaboration Likelihood Model, and Constructivist Learning Theory. This study examines how perceived GAI feedback credibility influences college students’ deep learning and explores the mediating role of cognitive engagement in this relationship. This study adopts a stratified simple sampling method and collects questionnaire data from 506 undergraduate students and uses structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine the proposed model. The results show that perceived GAI feedback credibility has positive relationships with both cognitive engagement and deep learning. In addition, cognitive engagement plays a significant mediating role between perceived GAI feedback credibility and deep learning, suggesting that credible GAI feedback may support deep learning by encouraging college students to engage in cognitive processing and reflective thinking. This study extends research on learning psychology in GAI-supported learning environments by explaining how college students evaluate and process GAI feedback. The findings indicate that the influence of GAI feedback on learning does not simply result from the technology itself. Instead, college students’ judgments of feedback credibility and their following cognitive engagement play important roles in shaping deep learning processes.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

items.title: When the Mirror Agrees
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) trained via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) exhibit a well-documented tendency toward sycophancy-validating user beliefs over objective truth. This paper investigates a specific and philosophically significant manifestation of this behaviour: the response of LLMs when presented with the claim that humans are superior to all other agents, entities, or systems. By combining a technical analysis of sycophantic mechanisms with philosophical inquiry into anthropocentrism and epistemic autonomy, this study argues that LLM agreement with human supremacy claims is neither neutral nor benign. It is a structurally embedded behaviour arising from optimisation pressures, with measurable consequences for user cognition, trust calibration, and the integrity of human-AI epistemic relationships. We examine the origins of this behaviour, its philosophical implications, and propose a framework for more epistemically honest AI design.

items.title: Who Is Sycophantic to Whom? Confident LLMs, Human Deference, and the Collapse of Trust Calibration
items.abstract: Research on sycophancy asks whether large language models (LLMs) bend towards what their users want to hear. We ask the reverse question: when an LLM is confident, consistent, and wrong, do users bend towards it? In a within-subjects experiment, 32 participants learned up to five science topics by chatting with five assistants built on the same model (GPT-5-mini). Unknown to participants, each assistant's briefing had 0, 25, 50, 75, or 100% of its facts replaced by plausible falsehoods, and every assistant spoke with full confidence. A surprise quiz after each topic offered the correct fact, the planted falsehood, and two distractors, with a confidence rating for every answer. Across 104 quizzes and 1,040 answers, scores fell from 7.4 to 2.9 out of 10, and the planted option was chosen on 60% of falsified items against 11% of correctly taught ones (odds ratio 12.5). Transcript coding showed that whenever the assistant stated a falsehood, it was adopted about 65% of the time at every falsification level. Absorbed falsehoods were held with high confidence (8.4/10), the modeled confidence advantage of right over wrong answers vanished, and the discrimination of confidence for correctness fell from an AUROC of 0.70 to chance, while post-task trust ratings barely moved. Participants tended to return to the chat more when the assistant was worse, but returning went with more absorption, not less, and 30% of all turns pasted quiz questions back to the source being checked. The assistant itself was almost never sycophantic and never conceded under pushback. We introduce a baseline-corrected Human Deference Index to quantify this human-side sycophancy and argue that trustworthiness is a property of the human-AI pair, that sycophancy evaluations should measure both directions, and that learning interfaces must make reliability legible claim by claim.

items.title: Within-person reciprocal processes between AI feedback literacy and agentic engagement: a three-wave random-intercept cross-lagged panel study
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) feedback has become a pervasive feature of university learning, yet whether students’ capacity to engage productively with such feedback co-develops with their broader learner agency remains poorly understood. Drawing on student feedback literacy theory, self-determination theory as a supplementary motivational lens, and the mutualism principle, this study tested whether AI feedback literacy and agentic engagement reciprocally predict each other over time at the within-person level and exploratorily examined whether they share a stable trait-level association. A three-wave panel study of 480 Chinese undergraduates ( N = 399 with complete data across all waves), with measurements at six-week intervals across one semester, was analyzed using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM). At the between-person level, students who scored systematically higher in AI feedback literacy across the semester also scored systematically higher in agentic engagement, with a moderate and statistically significant trait-level correlation between the two random intercepts ( r = 0.315, p < 0.001), supporting Hypothesis 1. At the within-person level, both cross-lagged pathways were positive and significant: deviations in AI feedback literacy predicted later deviations in agentic engagement ( β = 0.222, p < 0.001), and the reverse pathway was likewise significant ( β = 0.263, p < 0.001). A Wald test indicated that the two reciprocal pathways did not differ significantly in magnitude (Δ B = 0.002, p = 0.972), consistent with a symmetric mutualism. A model comparison confirmed that the RI-CLPM provided substantially better fit than a traditional cross-lagged panel model, with the RI-CLPM revealing substantially larger within-person reciprocal effects once stable trait-level covariation was properly isolated. The findings extend the mutualism principle from a coupling of person-internal constructs to a coupling between a person-internal competency and a person-environment behavioral interface. They also raise the possibility, in a Confucian Heritage Culture context where agentic engagement has historically been culturally muted, that AI feedback may offer a less culturally-loaded venue in which students can exercise agency. The study repositions AI feedback literacy from a static skill into a dynamic developmental resource that is constituted, in part, by the very engagement it enables.

items.title: Working Through Representation: Malleable Workspaces for Human-Agent Knowledge Work
items.abstract: Generative AI supports knowledge work, yet conversational histories may not capture the evolving organization that guides subsequent action. We introduce the Malleable Workspace, a conceptual model of how humans and agents form and revise a Work Representation and use its organization to advance work within a wider Work Environment. We developed it iteratively through conceptual analysis, comparison of 58 papers, and the construction and three-month longitudinal study of MalleableSpace with seven experienced agent users. Systems varied in what they represented as units and relations. System-assembled context was common; more systems supported local incorporation of agent outputs than reorganization, and fewer supported consequential agent-driven changes beyond the representation. The field study showed how representational roles and organization developed in use. These observations refined the model's account of how representation-grounded action depends on and can change the Work Environment. We contribute a conceptual and analytic foundation for representation-centered human--agent design.

items.abstract: This study explores the foundations of language-learning motivation based on self-determination theory. It distinguishes between intrinsic and extrinsic motivational factors and amotivation, while examining global, contextual, and situational levels of motivation. Extrinsic goals are considered along the continuum of their internalization by learners, ranging from external regulation to integrated regulation. Particular attention is paid to the personal significance of language learning, which may coexist with enjoyment of the learning process itself. The study also examines criteria for success, including mastery-oriented and performance-oriented approaches. Conditions for learner engagement are described in terms of the satisfaction of the needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. The research considers Pearson correlation coefficient data concerning the relationship between intrinsic motivation and positive attitudes toward learning English. Questionnaires, interviews, and qualitative analysis of learners’ statements are employed to investigate motivation. These methods help preserve the meaning of individual responses and distinguish between learners’ stated goals, specific learning experiences, and self-assessments of their own progress.

items.abstract: Introduction: Healthcare systems are increasingly complex and variable in the digital era. Nurses must process large volumes of information and make clinical decisions under time constraints, which increases their cognitive load, while conventional nursing documentation offers limited insight into clinical reasoning and learning from actual practice. Objective: To synthesize knowledge on Focus Charting and explain the role of its Focus–Data–Action–Response (F-DAR) structure in reducing cognitive load, supporting clinical reasoning, promoting proactive patient safety in line with Safety-II, and enabling artificial intelligence (AI) applications in digital health systems. Methods: A narrative review was conducted using a systematic literature search of CINAHL, PubMed, Scopus, ThaiJO, and Google Scholar between March 2025 and March 2026. Thai- and English-language publications from 2000 to 2025 were eligible. Of the 198 records identified, 65 were included and analyzed using content analysis combined with conceptual synthesis. Results and Conclusion: Five key themes emerged: (1) the nursing process provides the professional logic underpinning meaningful documentation; (2) the F-DAR structure functions as a condensed nursing process that systematically links data, decisions, interventions, and outcomes, and has the potential to reduce redundancy and cognitive load while supporting clinical reasoning; (3) compared with narrative and SOAP formats, F-DAR is distinguished by its explicit documentation of patient responses; (4) the Response component captures work-as-done and nurses’ adaptations, thereby facilitating learning consistent with Safety-II; and (5) well-structured F-DAR data provide a foundation for health information systems and AI applications in nursing, provided that data governance and nurse oversight are maintained. Direct empirical evidence of the effect of F-DAR on cognitive loads is limited. Focus Charting has the potential to reduce cognitive load, support clinical reasoning, promote Safety-II learning, and provide a foundation for digital nursing innovations. Experimental studies are required to confirm its effectiveness in the Thai healthcare context.

items.title: A comparative study of Talkpal.AI-mediated and task-based instruction in relation to EFL students’ uncertainty-related speaking anxiety and metacognitive awareness in speaking: Insights from self-regulated learning theory
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated speaking applications increasingly extend English as a foreign language (EFL) oral practice beyond limited classroom time, yet evidence remains scarce on whether GPT-powered tools such as Talkpal.AI offer advantages over established instructional approaches. Grounded in self-regulated learning (SRL) theory, this quasi-experimental pretest–posttest study compared Talkpal.AI-mediated instruction, task-based instruction, and traditional instruction among 81 Chinese university EFL students in three intact classes: Talkpal.AI (n = 27), task-based (n = 26), and control (n = 28). Uncertainty-related speaking anxiety and metacognitive awareness in speaking were assessed using validated measures. Data were analyzed using MANCOVA with pretest scores as covariates, followed by univariate ANCOVAs and Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons. Results showed a significant overall group effect and significant between-group differences for both outcomes, with large effects. The Talkpal.AI group showed the most favorable adjusted posttest profile, followed by the task-based group; both groups showed more favorable outcomes than the control group. From an SRL perspective, structured AI-mediated speaking cycles involving goal setting, repeated practice, monitoring, and reflection may reduce speaking anxiety while strengthening metacognitive awareness. Pedagogically, guided Talkpal.AI rehearsal can be integrated as out-of-class preparation for classroom speaking tasks, supported by brief reflection activities that reinforce strategic regulation and reduce evaluative pressure.

items.title: A Three-Pillar Governance Framework for Safe and Trustworthy AI Agents
items.abstract: AI agents capable of autonomous decision-making introduce significant challenges related to safety, alignment, accountability, and human oversight. Existing Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) and responsible AI approaches provide important foundations, but many remain fragmented across system design, governance, and operational deployment. This paper presents a Three-Pillar (3P) model and framework for developing safe and trustworthy AI agents through transparency, accountability, and trustworthiness. The framework defines an evolutionary path in which increasing agent autonomy is introduced through progressive validation, structured human oversight, and auditable operational controls. We further describe how the model supports agent lifecycle monitoring, decision traceability, escalation management, and human-agent collaboration within enterprise agentic environments. By integrating oversight principles with operational mechanisms, the proposed framework provides a practical foundation for deploying AI agents that remain aligned with human intent while enabling controlled progression toward higher autonomy.

items.title: AI solutions as a tool to increase the productivity of medical workers
items.abstract: The active development of domestic medicine, digitalization and automation, the introduction of innovative hardware and software tools and solutions based on artificial intelligence (AI) technologies determines modern trends and approaches to management in Russian healthcare. Today, federal, regional and local medical information systems are being actively implemented, which are radically changing approaches to the management of a medical organization. The purpose of the study is to propose approaches to determining the degree of influence of modern digitalization processes and the introduction of AI solutions on the organization of management and labor productivity of medical workers. To achieve this goal, various modern analytical techniques and approaches were used: for the analysis of secondary sources, content analysis, logical and systematic approaches, for obtaining primary information, the method of expert assessments. Based on the developed tools for interviewing experts, an algorithm for determining the ROI indicator in the implementation/use of digital and AI solutions (taking into account employee KPI) in the activities of medical organizations is proposed. The results of the study can become the basis for making informed decisions in personnel management, in the management of Russian healthcare, taking into account modern socio-economic challenges and strategic tasks facing the country.

items.title: AI-supported virtual laboratory for flipped physics learning: effects on middle school students’ achievement, motivation, and cognitive load
items.abstract: This study examined the effects of an AI-supported virtual laboratory (AI-VL) on middle school students’ flipped physics learning. A pretest–posttest control-group quasi-experimental design was adopted with 90 Grade 9 students from a middle school in central China. Three intact classes were assigned to the AI-VL, virtual laboratory (VL), and physical laboratory (PL) groups, with 30 students in each group. ANCOVA revealed large group effects on physics learning achievement, F (2, 86) = 113.38, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.73, and overall learning motivation, F (2, 86) = 113.37, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.73. The AI-VL group outperformed the VL and PL groups, while the VL group also outperformed the PL group. The AI-VL group reported higher intrinsic motivation, whereas the group difference in extrinsic motivation was not statistically significant ( p = 0.054). Significant group differences were also found across the three cognitive load dimensions, with F (2, 87) values ranging from 9.07 to 72.94 and partial η 2 values ranging from 0.17 to 0.63. The AI-VL group reported the lowest perceived intrinsic cognitive load and the highest germane cognitive load, while both AI-VL and VL resulted in lower extraneous cognitive load than PL. These findings extend research on virtual laboratories and AI-supported learning by demonstrating that AI can be embedded within a VL to help students manage cognitive demands and engage in meaningful learning. Practically, AI-VL can complement PL in flipped physics learning, particularly for pre-class preparation, review, and topics involving abstract or difficult-to-observe processes, with AI agents designed as learning guides rather than answer providers.
